Within this repeated process of combining and reshaping traditions, the Greek mythical element remains strongly present in the structure of Arab legendary narrative. Yet through the force of storytelling and continual adaptation, it eventually became thoroughly Arab. The legend of Zarqa al-Yamama is, in fact, an echo of Greek stories and myths, some of them connected with the Trojan War. The Arab tribes appear to have heard these stories again and again. Al-A'sha may even have imitated the Iliad, retelling Greek legendary material in verse as the story of the prophetess Zarqa. This is what I shall try to show here.
4. The Wars of Alexander the Great and the Legend of Zarqaʾ al-Yamama

One Greek story, forming part of the wider cycle of legends surrounding the Trojan War, tells of Cassandra, daughter of Priam, king of Troy, and his wife Hecuba. Cassandra became the victim of Apollo's anger. The god fell passionately in love with her and, because of that love, gave her the gift of prophecy. At first Cassandra appears to have promised to return Apollo's love. But she soon became afraid that she might lose her prophetic gift, broke her promise, and withdrew from him. Apollo immediately took revenge by ensuring that no one would ever believe her prophecies.
4. The Wars of Alexander the Great and the Legend of Zarqaʾ al-Yamama

When the Greeks attacked Troy, Cassandra warned the inhabitants that the enemy was approaching. No one was prepared to believe her. The Greek heroes were therefore able to enter Troy while Cassandra's prophetic power had, for all practical purposes, been rendered useless.
4. The Wars of Alexander the Great and the Legend of Zarqaʾ al-Yamama

Here, then, is the Greek counterpart of Zarqa al-Yamama: Cassandra. Her original image was blended with similar figures, or figures derived from it, including Zarqa bint Zuhayr, the great prophetess of Hajar. Within the historical narratives, tribal wars between Tasm and Jadis in al-Yamama were then imagined anew. In the crude machinery of the new legend, the conflict came to appear as though it had really taken place in the time of Hassan Yuha'min, and as though he had crucified a young woman called Zarqa al-Yamama.

The storyteller in this case was Jubayr ibn al-Hasan. Al-Nasa'i regarded him as a weak transmitter, while al-Sijistani also questioned him because of the weakness of his transmission of hadith. Yet he did more than repeat the old legend. He introduced new elements into it. Remembering the prophetess of Hajar—and al-Yamama, his own homeland, as we have already seen—he merged her image once again with that of Cassandra, who warned the Trojans but was not believed.

This suggests that Ibn al-Hasan, or perhaps one of the other transmitters of the story, may himself have heard the Greek legend. And why not? Hajar, whose great historic capital was Gerrha, was according to the Greek geographer Strabo, who visited it, one of the wealthiest and most important cities of its age. Greek merchants were constantly present in its markets.

A modern reader need not find the following possibility surprising: Jubayr ibn al-Hasan may have heard a Greek version of the Trojan War in al-Yamama or in its flourishing markets. A large Greek community once lived in Arabia along the Red Sea coast and around the port of Aden. In time, this community was absorbed into the Arab tribes. Yet its culture, memories, and perhaps even its myths need not have disappeared with it. They may instead have survived by being repeatedly merged with new stories transmitted by later settlers.

We have a particularly good example of this kind of settlement. The Yemeni island of Socotra was home not only to Arab and Indian communities, but also to a Greek one. Greeks had reached the south-west of the Arabian Peninsula by sea during the military campaigns of Alexander the Great, around 336 BC. Al-Hamdani, the Yemeni historian, estimated their number at ten thousand fighting men and said that they later converted to Christianity.

The author of the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, however, believed that the presence of this Greek community was partly the result of a Ptolemaic campaign against the port of Aden, after which a number of Greek families were settled there. Could the legend of Cassandra, then, have taken root in Arabia more than a thousand years before Hassan's campaign against the tribes of Ma'add?

One final point remains. The intensity and effectiveness of this continual blending of images within classical Arab legendary narrative can be seen especially clearly in the presence of elements belonging to Sumerian mythology. In the Epic of Gilgamesh, for example, we can find what appears to be the original model for the Arab king Imlīq, who is, of course, a non-historical figure. The epic tells us:

He brought shame and corruption upon the city, burdening the unfortunate city with abuses and forced labour. They sounded the drum for the king of Uruk, city of the great marketplaces, so that at its call he might choose whatever bride he desired. For Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, city of the great marketplaces, the drum was sounded so that he might choose brides before their husbands and be the first bridegroom before the man they were to marry.

The echo of these successive images can surely be heard, in some form, in the legendary world of The Thousand and One Nights, where the killing of brides each night becomes an even more explicit symbolic representation of defloration. Shahriyar kills his bride every night. The Arab Imlīq and the Sumerian Gilgamesh perform a symbolically similar act by taking the virginity of brides before their weddings.

Several layers of material—ancient Arab, Sumerian, and later Greek—therefore helped shape the legendary narrative surrounding Zarqa al-Yamama. Ultimately, these layers point back to genuine historical reports that have been transformed into myth: reports of a relatively late Yemeni military campaign against the northern tribes of Ma'add.
